title: Signal Quality and Impedance
subtitle: Check the measurement before training the person
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating signal quality and impedance within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain signal quality and impedance without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in signal quality and impedance.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to signal quality and impedance.

sections.explainSimply: Impedance describes how well the electrode contact conducts changing electrical signals.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Low and balanced impedances reduce susceptibility to noise, although acceptable ranges depend on amplifier design. Live signal inspection remains essential.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: High-input-impedance amplifiers tolerate higher absolute impedance, but large asymmetry can increase common-mode contamination. Quantitative thresholds should follow manufacturer and laboratory standards.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Trying to tune a faint radio station: contact, interference and antenna placement determine what reaches the speaker.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand signal quality and impedance to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A green impedance indicator does not prove the waveform is artifact-free.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using signal quality and impedance predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A green impedance indicator does not prove the waveform is artifact-free. Evidence classification: established acquisition principle.
